https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/19/korr.text: Menü Kereső Házkutatást tartottak több ukrán magas rangú tisztviselő otthonában Külföld Dezső András Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Kiterjedt műveletet indított az Ukrán Nemzeti Korrupcióellenes Iroda (NABU). A hatóságok magas rangú tisztségviselőknél, parlamenti képviselőknél és az állami tulajdonú Sense Banknál tartottak házkutatást egy bűnszervezet felszámolása és pénzmosás gyanúja miatt – írja a Kyiv Independent . A NABU augusztus 19-én közölte, hogy nagyszabású akciót folytat egy olyan bűnszervezet leleplezésének érdekében, amelyet egy jelenlegi és egy korábbi ukrán parlamenti képviselő vezet, és amelyben az Elnöki Hivatal magas rangú tisztségviselői is érintettek. A hatósági akció során házkutatást tartottak többek között Irina Mudra, az Elnöki Hivatal helyettes vezetője, valamint Vadim Stolar parlamenti képviselő otthonában. Stolar a közösségi oldalán megerősítette a házkutatást, hangsúlyozva, hogy mindenben együttműködik a hatóságokkal. Irina Mudra – Fotó: Jeroen Jumelet (AFP) A nyomozás szálai elérik a korábbi parlamenti képviselőt Makszim Mikitaszt, valamint az állami tulajdonú Sense Bankot is, ahol szintén átkutatták a helyiségeket. A hatóságok gyanúja szerint a gyanúsítottak mintegy 150 millió hrivnyát (kb. 3,4 millió dollárt) moshattak tisztára. Ezt az összeget korábban óvadékként tették le a hírhedt „Midasz-hadművelet” egyik kulcsszereplőjéért, Herman Halusenko volt igazságügyi és energiaügyi miniszterért. Halusenko ellen az állami atomenergia-vállalatot, az Energoatomot érintő, mintegy 100 millió dolláros korrupciós séma miatt folytatnak eljárást pénzmosás és szervezett bűnözés vádjával. A „Midasz-hadműveletként” ismert ügy Volodimir Zelenszkij elnökségének eddigi legnagyobb korrupciós botránya. A kiszivárgott bírósági végzések szerint a Sense Bankot használták csatornaként az óvadékhoz szükséges pénzeszközök egy részének átutalására, megkerülve a pénzügyi monitoringkövetelményeket. A nyomozók szerint Irina Mudrának kellett megszerveznie a 150 millió hrivnyás óvadék összegyűjtését. Ezen felül az Elnöki Hivatal nem azonosított szereplői azzal is megbízták Mudrát – aki az elnöki stábban a bírósági rendszerért és az igazságügyi reformokért felel –, hogy vonja a Sense Bankot az Elnöki Hivatal közvetlen befolyása alá, megakadályozva, hogy más állami szervek szerezzenek felette ellenőrzést. A NABU által közzétett hangfelvételek tanúsága szerint Mudra még júniusban maga számolt be arról, hogy a bank vezérigazgatója és az igazgatóság elnöke az ő közvetítésével lépett kapcsolatba az elnöki stábbal. Korábban írtuk, hogy májusban két hónapra előzetes letartóztatásba helyezték Zelenszkij egykor legbefolyásosabb emberét , Andrij Jermakot. Az ukrán elnöki hivatal november végén lemondott vezetője a gyanú szerint több mint 10 millió dollár értékű pénzmosásban érintett a volt kormányfő-helyettessel, Olekszij Csernisovval és Zelenszkij régi barátjával, Timur Mindiccsel együtt. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: The government has taken a strict approach to people in Gaza who hope to reunite with family members in the UK. Photograph: Ramadan Abed/Reuters View image in fullscreen The government has taken a strict approach to people in Gaza who hope to reunite with family members in the UK. Photograph: Ramadan Abed/Reuters Immigration and asylum Court quashes block on mothers and children in Gaza joining families in UK Immigration court judge finds ‘unsafe journeys’ policy was applied unlawfully to two families Diane Taylor Sun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 10.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A decision by the Home Office to block mothers and children in Gaza from joining their families in the UK has been quashed by a court. Families abroad who have had their applications approved to reunite with loved ones in the UK usually have to undergo biometric checks, including fingerprinting and facial images at a visa application centre. But the VAC in Gaza has been closed since October 2023 and it is difficult to get out of the territory. The government has an unsafe journeys policy that offers some flexibility in this kind of situation, but has taken a more strict approach to families – often mothers with very young children – in Gaza who are hoping to reunite with husbands and fathers granted refugee status in the UK. A judge in the immigration court known as the upper tribunal has found the home secretary acted unlawfully in the way the policy was applied to two families and has quashed the decision to block them. Both are young mothers with five children between them aged seven and under, hoping to reunite with their husbands who have been granted refugee status in the UK. Both families are living in dire straits in tents in Gaza with insufficient food, no access to clean water, rodents, mosquitoes, bedbugs and the risk of snipers. The Home Office says it is looking to appeal against the decision. An estimated 250-300 people in Gaza who want to reunite with immediate family members who have been granted refugee status in the UK are similarly stranded . The Home Office says biometrics should be obtained before families travel. The Foreign Office has said it is willing to evacuate some of these families from Gaza so they can obtain biometrics in Jordan. In her judgment, the judge, Fiona Lindsley, said the families were living in vulnerable structures in a war zone, malnourished, unwell and struggling psychologically with anxiety from their husbands and fathers in the UK that they willwould not survive much longer if they remained in Gaza. “The best interests of these children should be the primary consideration, and it cannot be in their best interests to be afraid, undernourished and suffering from diseases of poverty and insanitary conditions without their fathers and no end in sight to that separation,” she said. Decla Palmer, a solicitor at Greater Manchester Immigration Aid Unit who represents the families, said: “The Home Office is doing everything possible to delay and to defend its unlawful decisions, taking a policy position that blocks people in Gaza who are eligible to come to the UK from being able to do so. “These families are completely broken – it is difficult to put into words the trauma they have faced and continue to endure. The mothers and children, trapped in Gaza, are suffering each and every day. The fathers, in the UK, are facing the prospect that they may never hold their children again. The Home Office is actively keeping these families apart, leaving them stranded in Gaza in grave danger.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion On Monday, the Home Office announced refugee resettlement routes including for Palestinian refugees and women from Afghanistan. However, this scheme processes only a few hundred applications each year. It is not known when the much larger refugee family reunion scheme will restart, after it was suspended in September 2025. The Refugee Council estimates that since then approximately 20,000 people have been denied family reunion. Initially, the government indicated that new refugee family reunion rules would be introduced in the spring of 2025, but the scheme remains suspended. Home Office sources have indicated that no further details will be announced about this safe and legal lifeline for refugees to reach the UK until 2027. A Home Office spokesperson said: “We will be looking to appeal this decision. Biometrics, including fingerprints and facial images, are a core part of the UK’s immigration system, and their enrolment at a UK overseas visa application centre is a standard requirement when making a visa application to come to the UK. “The enrolment of biometrics enables comprehensive checks against UK and international immigration and criminal records to identify individuals who may pose a threat to national security, public safety or immigration controls, or who are likely to breach UK laws if admitted.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum Home Office Shabana Mahmood Gaza Palestine Israel-Gaza war news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Israel does not have right to close UK consulate in Jerusalem, Foreign Office advised British banks warned not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban begins Inquest into British aid workers killed in Gaza may call on Israeli and UK military chiefs UK sanctions on Israel ‘fall far short’ of its obligations, legal experts say Burnham to face pressure at Labour conference to recognise Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide Benjamin Netanyahu describes UK as ‘first Islamic republic to get a nuclear weapon’ Led By Donkeys wins compensation over seizure of Gaza protest banner UK government has failed Palestinian people, says senior Labour MP UK government urged to act over proposed illegal Israeli settlement British Museum removes word ‘Palestine’ from some displays Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://blueprint.ng/dicon-fg-seeks-tech.text: Spread the word The Minister of State for Defence, Dr. Bello Muhammed Matawalle, has embarked on a 3-day official working visit to the Czech Republic to strengthen defence industrial cooperation between Nigeria and the Czech Republic. This was disclosed in a statement by (CIO) Information & Public Relations,Queeneth Iheoma-Hart. According to the statement, the Minister, who led a delegation comprising senior officials of the Ministry of Defence, the Defence Industries Corporation of Nigeria (DICON) and the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure (NASENI), attended the Czech Air Force Day/Air Show and Defence Exhibition in Ostrava, where modern and heavy defence equipment produced by the Czech defence industry were on display. On the sidelines of the exhibition, Dr. Matawalle held a strategic bilateral meeting with his counterpart, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence of the Czech Republic, Lt. Gen. Jaromír Zuna (Rtd). Discussions at the meeting centred on strengthening the existing strategic partnership and deepening collaboration and cooperation between the Federal Republic of Nigeria and the Czech Republic towards enhancing the manufacturing and production capacity of DICON in the area of military hardware production. Minister Matawalle specifically stressed the need for the Czech Republic to partner with DICON to establish an ammunition production line in Nigeria. The issue of Transfer of Technology (ToT) to Nigeria, particularly in Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) and other military hardware, was also extensively discussed by both Ministers. In his response, the Czech Minister of Defence expressed delight over the visit and assured the Honourable Minister of State of the Czech Republic’s readiness and willingness to collaborate with and support Nigeria in enhancing DICON’s defence production capabilities, including the requisite transfer of technology. As part of the visit, the Minister is also scheduled to tour several Defence and Security industrial complexes across the Czech Republic. https://www.heraldscotland.com/opinion/2.text: David Lonsdale Retail Retail Crime Business Economy Scotland Scottish retailers urge tougher action on rising crime Retail Retail Crime Business Economy Scotland By David Lonsdale Share 0 Comments Shoplifting and threats towards retail workers remain a growing concern for retailers across Scotland (Image: NQ Staff) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Whenever I visit shopkeepers, one issue dominates: crime – particularly theft and the threats and abuse towards brilliant and passionate staff that often accompany it. Thieves are said to be more brazen and aggressive. This is despite record spending by retailers on crime prevention and legislation – introduced by Daniel Johnson MSP and enacted five years ago – to better protect shopworkers. That record spending has seen stores deploy body-worn cameras, more security guards, enhanced CCTV, anti-theft devices and new crime reporting systems. The enormous cost is borne by retailers and by customers through higher prices. Read more: Shoplifting tops 53,000 offences as retail crime climbs Official shoplifting figures continue to spiral, rising 88% over the past three years. In the past year theft from stores increased by a fifth to 57,000 incidents – 165 every day. Scottish Retail Consortium research suggests the true picture is far worse. With 22,500 shops, the idea that each store experienced fewer than three incidents on average over the year is far-fetched. Theft is a key driver of the despicable rise in abuse and threats towards store workers. Thanks to Mr Johnson’s legislation, we have a clearer sense of the scale: in the past year there were 3,900 incidents of threatening or abusive behaviour towards shopworkers and 3,200 assaults. Nine times a day shopworkers are being physically assaulted, which is totally unacceptable. A separate SRC-Opinium survey found one in five Scots had witnessed theft or abuse of shop staff over the past year . Crime has become an all-too-common part of the shopping experience – deterring Scots from visiting retail destinations and impacting the health of high streets. CCTV footage of an alleged shoplifting incident in a Scottish convenience store. Retailers say theft, abuse and threats against staff remain a growing concern (Image: Village Shop Longniddry) To its credit, John Swinney ’s Government has listened to our representations and given the issue greater priority. Dedicated funding enabled Police Scotland to establish a Retail Crime Taskforce in April 2025. Eighteen months on, the results are encouraging: more proactive work in retail crime hotspots; more arrests of persistent offenders; better evidence-sharing systems; and recovery of stolen goods. Investment in online crime-reporting systems is making it quicker for police and stores to gather CCTV footage and witness statements. The new reporting system helps explain some of this year’s increase in shoplifting whilst giving a more accurate reflection of the extent of the problem. So far, so good. But to turn the tide on retail crime, much more must be done. Read more: Retail crime has risen to unacceptable levels across the UK First, Ministers are currently reviewing their strategic policing priorities. The refresh should include an explicit, enduring commitment to tackling retail crime – not just a temporary taskforce. Second, funding for the taskforce should be increased in the Scottish Budget and maintained until theft has fallen consistently. After all, reported thefts have leapt 40% since funding was first unveiled. Third, action must extend across the criminal justice system, including the courts. Those who steal from stores need to know they will not only be caught but face consequences. Fast-track court proceedings should be considered for prolific offenders. 'Let’s call it what it is: stealing and thieving' (Image: NQ) A common trigger for intimidation and abuse is retail workers doing what the state increasingly requires of them. New in-store regulations on vapes are in the pipeline and will need implemented by staff, while Ministers want to legislate for price caps on food products across several thousand grocery stores. These measures can put retail workers on the frontline of customer frustration. Hungary’s price caps led to shortages and created flashpoints between customers and staff. Government must explain clearly why such measures are being introduced – and make equally clear that abusive behaviour isn’t tolerated. Politicians, too, should mind their language towards the sector and avoid the type of invective heard when price caps were first unveiled during the election. Read more: Call to make shops in Scotland keep vapes and nicotine pouches hidden The narrative around shoplifting must also change. The word doesn’t convey the seriousness of the crime, still less its cumulative impact. Let’s call it what it is: stealing and thieving. Retailers are playing their part by investing in measures to detect and deter criminals, but more need to up their game and report all incidents. This will give the police the fullest possible picture and should mean more resource is allocated. If shopkeepers felt there was little point previously in reporting incidents then the work of the taskforce should help disabuse them of that notion. Finally, each of us needs to be more considerate towards retail workers. We all have a role in reducing retail crime and making the shopping experience and retail destinations safer. David Lonsdale is director of the Scottish Retail Consortium. Retail Retail Crime Business Economy Scotland Share 0 Comments Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading... https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq3d.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, The latest talks between Putin (right) and Witkoff lasted about three hours in St Petersburg By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 21 October 2026, 16:56 BST Updated 3 hours ago Russia is "ready in principle" to resume talks with the US and Ukraine on ending the conflict, Vladimir Putin's top aide has said. Yuri Ushakov was speaking after Putin met US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff in the Russian city of St Petersburg. Ushakov said a new round could be held next month, and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky later said he wanted this to happen as soon as possible. Kyiv and its European allies have long been pressing Moscow for resumption of the talks halted in February. Russia has for months refused as it believes it is winning on the battlefield with Ukraine facing an acute shortage of interceptors against deadly Russian missile attacks. Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Monday. It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after talks in Oslo that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed. Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful". Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war that began in February 2022 when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption. Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict." A US official later told the BBC that Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key negotiator, had proposed at Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital "a trilateral meeting at the technical level between the US, Russia, and Ukraine". "This was accepted by the Ukrainians in Oslo yesterday and by the Russians in St Petersburg today," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. Late on Wednesday, Zelensky told reporters: "We received feedback that Russia... supports a trilateral meeting between our teams. The American side is proposing to do this as soon as possible. We are in favour of it." Ushakov also told reporters that President Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative". Ukraine and its European allies are disputing Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front. On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line. "We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this. Figure caption, Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now" Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come." The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US. Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine". Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran. He was heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace". That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier. Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move. Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now". Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions by the US satellite internet network Starlink which is owned by Elon Musk which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia. US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation. Image source, Truth Social Image caption, Hubbard had been in jail in Russia for allegedly fighting for Ukraine Before the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine. Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release. When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage. "Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said and about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."
